newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Bahia cocoa producers give blessing to imports.
newsitem.headline: Bahia cocoa producers give blessing to imports.

text.p: Bahian cocoa producers accept there may be a deficit of up to 250,000 60-kg bags (15,000 tonnes) in the midcrop and have given their blessing to a group of companies to import cocoa, a producer official said.

"We had a meeting today in which we agreed that there may be a shortfall of up to 250,000 bags and so we accepted the need to import cocoa up to August," said Wallace Setenta, president of the National Cocoa Producers Council (CNPC).

The group of four companies seeking to import cocoa are the Brazilian arms of Swiss food giant Nestle SA and Cargill Inc of the U.S., grinders Chadler and Joanes Industrias, a subsidiary of the U.K.'s E.D. and F. Man.

"We discussed with the CNPC that given a probable midcrop of 900,000 bags, the lowest in 23 years, it was clear there will be shortage of cocoa," said the group's spokesman Wady Jasmin, who is president of Joanes.
"The CNPC accepted the need for and was absolutely favorable to the idea of imports," he added.
The group is now waiting to hear from the Agriculture Ministry as what should be the next step to fulfill legal requirements.
Following the problematic importation of 5,000 tonnes of Ivorian beans two years ago, the government issued a decree allowing the import of cocoa but under numerous conditions.

A small company last year imported an experimental cargo of cocoa from Indonesia after Agriculture Ministry technicians certified that Indonesian cocoa did not pose any threat of pest or plague, Jasmin said.
For the time being Indonesia is the only country that has been pre-certified which means that it will be the most likely origin for imports this year, Jasmin said.
"The only thing is at this stage I don't think supply from Indonesia will be more than 4,000 to 6,000 tonnes," Jasmin said,
The group has not yet agreed any purchase given it is awaiting orientation from the Agriculture Ministry.
"We have negotiated some options but we can only finalise deals when we receive clear indications from the Ministry of Agriculture," Jasmin said.

"Ideally this cocoa should be loaded at the end of March as it takes 60 days to arrive from Indonesia and so would only arrive at the end of May, beginning of June which we estimate will be the peak of the supply shortage," he added.
Dry weather in the Bahia region through December and January has meant it is unlikely there will be any midcrop cocoa until late June or July whereas normally the harvest begins in May.
The actual level of imports will depend on the size of the midcrop, Jasmin said.

"If the midcrop turns out to be a little better than we anticipated, then perhaps 6,000 to 8,000 tonnes will do. But otherwise on the basis of a 900,000 bag midcrop, we will need up to 15,000 tonnes," he said.
An import committee has been formed to monitor the process, with seven representatives covering producers, local and federal government and the industry, Setenta said.
